questm1-name-formula#2.en: Look at the faces: flat polygons make a prism/pyramid; a curved face means a cylinder, cone or sphere.

questm1-name-formula#4.en: A ${correct} — read it off the faces and the cross-section.

questm1-name-formula#5.en: Which is the correct volume formula for this ${s.name}?

questm1-name-formula#6.en: Volume fills the inside (cubic units). Prisms & cylinders: base area × height. Cones & pyramids: a third of that.

questm1-name-formula#9.en: Which is the correct total surface area formula for this closed ${s.name}?

questm1-name-formula#10.en: Surface area adds up every outside face (square units). Curved faces unroll: a cylinder's side becomes a 2πr × h rectangle.

questm1-name-formula#11.en: Total surface area of a closed ${s.name} = ${s.sa}.

questm1-name-formula#13.en: For any prism or a cylinder, is the volume always (area of the base) × (perpendicular height)?

questm1-name-formula#14.en: A prism keeps the same cross-section all the way up, so you just stack the base area through the height.

questm1-name-formula#15.en: Yes — for a prism or cylinder, V = base area × height.

questm1-name-formula#16.en: Same cross-section all the way up → V = A_base × H.

questm1-name-formula#17.en: A cone holds how much of a cylinder that has the same base and height?

questm1-name-formula#22.en: Cones and pyramids are the ‘pointy’ third — V = ⅓ × (matching prism or cylinder).

questm1-name-formula#23.en: ⅓ — a cone is ⅓ of the cylinder with the same base and height, so V = ⅓πr²H.

questm2-heights#5.en: For the volume of this ${shape} (${vol}), which height do you use?

questm2-heights#8.en: neither; you use the radius r

questm2-heights#9.en: neither; you use the base side ℓ

questm2-heights#11.en: Volume is about how much fills the inside, so you need the true straight-up height H, not the longer slanted one.

questm2-heights#12.en: The perpendicular height H — it runs straight from the apex down to the centre of the base.

questm2-heights#13.en: V = ${vol} uses the perpendicular height H (the dashed line down the middle).

questm2-heights#16.en: For the ${face} of this ${shape}, which height do you use?

questm2-heights#19.en: The slanted face lies along the slope, so its area needs the length measured along that slope — the slant height h.

questm2-heights#20.en: The slant height h — it runs along the sloping face, from the apex to the edge of the base.

questm2-heights#21.en: The sloping face is measured with the slant height h, not the perpendicular H.

questm2-heights#22.en: from the apex, down the sloping side, to the rim of the base

questm2-heights#23.en: from the apex, down the middle of a triangular face, to a base edge

questm2-heights#24.en: On this diagram, which length is the slant height h?

questm2-heights#26.en: the dashed line straight down the middle

questm2-heights#27.en: the line across the base (the radius / side)

questm2-heights#28.en: the longest edge of the whole solid

questm2-heights#29.en: h is the one drawn along the slope; the dashed straight-down line is the perpendicular height H.

questm2-heights#30.en: The slant height h is the slanting line ${desc}.

questm2-heights#31.en: h = slant (along the face); H = perpendicular (dashed, straight down).

questm2-heights#32.en: Is the slant height h always longer than the perpendicular height H?

questm2-heights#33.en: h, H and the radius form a right-angled triangle with h as the hypotenuse (h² = H² + r²).

questm2-heights#34.en: Yes — h is the hypotenuse of the right triangle h² = H² + r², so h > H.

questm2-heights#35.en: h² = H² + r²  →  h is the hypotenuse, so it is the longest of the three.

questm2-heights#36.en: All lengths on a solid are in cm. Its volume is measured in …

questm2-heights#37.en: All lengths on a solid are in cm. Its surface area is measured in …

questm2-heights#42.en: Area covers a flat region (length × length → squared); volume fills space (length × length × length → cubed).

questm2-heights#43.en: Volume is a cubic measure → cm³.

questm2-heights#44.en: Surface area is a square measure → cm².

questm3-open#2.en: Look at the diagram. Which formula gives this cylinder's total surface area?

questm3-open#3.en: Start with the curved side 2πrh (always there). Then add one circle πr² for each end that is closed — a solid lid, not an open rim.

questm3-open#13.en: Look at the top of this cylinder. Do you include the top circle in its surface area?

questm3-open#14.en: A solid lid is a real surface to count; an open rim you can see into has no lid there to cover.

questm3-open#15.en: Yes — the top is a closed lid, so its circle counts: + πr².

questm3-open#16.en: No — the top is open, so there is no top circle to include.

questm3-open#17.en: Closed top (solid lid) → count its circle: + πr².

questm3-open#18.en: Open top → leave out πr² for the top; only count ends that are closed.

questm3-open#19.en: This pipe is open at both ends. Which surface(s) make up its outer area?

questm3-open#22.en: the curved side + one circle → πr² + 2πrh

questm3-open#24.en: No lids at all — you can see straight through. So no circles are counted.

questm3-open#25.en: Just the curved side, 2πrh — a pipe has no closed ends.

questm3-open#27.en: A rectangular fish tank is open at the top (no lid). How many faces make up the glass surface?

questm3-open#32.en: A closed box has 6 faces. Remove the lid and one face is gone.

questm3-open#33.en: 5 — the base and the 4 sides; the top (lid) is left out.

questm4-composite#3.en: For the total surface area, do you include the dashed circle where the ${topName} sits on the cylinder?

questm4-composite#4.en: That circle is sealed inside the solid — no one could paint it. Joined faces are left out.

questm4-composite#5.en: No — the joining face is hidden inside, so it is not part of the outer surface.

questm4-composite#6.en: Two solids joined → add the outer surfaces, omit the shared (hidden) face.

questm4-composite#7.en: What is the total volume of this silo (a cylinder with a cone on top)?

questm4-composite#12.en: Add the two parts: cylinder (πr²h) plus cone (⅓πr²H). h is the cylinder height, H the cone height.

questm4-composite#13.en: Add the parts: cylinder πr²h + cone ⅓πr²H.

questm4-composite#17.en: What is the total volume of this tank (a cylinder with a hemisphere on top)?

questm4-composite#22.en: A hemisphere is HALF a sphere, so ½ × 4/3·πr³ = ⅔πr³. Add it to the cylinder πr²h.

questm4-composite#26.en: Which surfaces add up to the total surface area of this silo (closed flat bottom, cone on top)?

questm4-composite#27.en: bottom circle + cylinder's curved side + cone's slanted surface

questm4-composite#28.en: bottom circle + cylinder's curved side + cone's slanted surface + the join circle

questm4-composite#29.en: two circles + cylinder's curved side + cone's slanted surface

questm4-composite#30.en: cylinder's curved side + cone's slanted surface only

questm4-composite#31.en: Count every OUTSIDE face: the base, the wrapping cylinder wall, the cone's slope. The circle where they join is hidden.

questm4-composite#32.en: Base circle + cylinder side + cone slant. The cylinder's top is covered by the cone, so it is left out.

questm4-composite#33.en: outer faces only: πr² (base) + 2πrh (cylinder side) + πr·(slant) (cone)

questm4-composite#34.en: To find the volume of a composite solid, do you add the volumes of its parts?

questm4-composite#35.en: Volume is just how much space is filled, so the parts simply add up — nothing is hidden for volume.

questm4-composite#36.en: Yes — total volume = sum of the parts' volumes.

questm5-mixed#3.en: Flat faces only → prism or pyramid. A curved face → cylinder, cone, sphere or hemisphere.

questm5-mixed#6.en: Prisms/cylinder: base × height. Cone/pyramid: ⅓ of that. Sphere 4/3·πr³, hemisphere half of it.

questm5-mixed#9.en: Pick the total surface area formula for this closed ${s.name}.

questm5-mixed#10.en: Add every outside face. Curved sides unroll into rectangles; round ends are circles.

questm5-mixed#15.en: Read the diagram — which surface-area formula fits this cylinder?

questm5-mixed#16.en: Curved side 2πrh always; add πr² for each CLOSED end.

questm5-mixed#18.en: Every dimension of a solid is multiplied by ${k}. Its volume becomes how many times as big?

questm5-mixed#19.en: Volume uses three lengths, so it scales by k × k × k = k³.

questm5-mixed#22.en: Every dimension of a solid is multiplied by ${k}. Its surface area becomes how many times as big?

questm5-mixed#23.en: Area uses two lengths, so it scales by k × k = k².

questm6-height#1.en: Calculate the perpendicular height H of this cone.

questm6-height#2.en: Build the rearranged equation for H². Tap a piece to drop it into the next box.

questm6-height#3.en: The slant is the hypotenuse, so it goes first and stands alone.

questm6-height#5.en: Square the slant, square r, then subtract.

questm6-height#8.en: r, H and the slant h make a right-angled triangle with the slant as the hypotenuse: h² = H² + r². So H = √(h² − r²).

questm6-height#10.en: h² = H² + r²  →  H² = h² − r²

questm6-height#14.en: Calculate the slant height h of this cone.

questm6-height#15.en: Build the Pythagoras equation for h². Tap a piece to drop it into the next box.

questm6-height#16.en: Addition commutes — H² and r² can go in either box.

questm6-height#18.en: Square H, square r, then add.

questm6-height#20.en: The slant is the hypotenuse, so it sits alone: h² = H² + r², giving h = √(H² + r²).

questm6-height#26.en: Calculate the perpendicular height H of this square-based pyramid.

questm6-height#28.en: Divide the full base ℓ by 2.

questm6-height#29.en: Build the equation for H², using HALF the base you just found. Tap a piece to drop it into the next box.

questm6-height#30.en: The slant is the hypotenuse. The bottom leg is HALF the base — the whole base is on the pad to tempt you.

questm6-height#31.en: Square the slant, square half the base, then subtract.

questm6-height#32.en: The slant h, the height H and HALF the base (ℓ/2) form a right triangle: h² = H² + (ℓ/2)². Use HALF the base, not the whole side!

questm6-height#35.en: the bottom leg is HALF the base

questm6-height#38.en: For a cone, how are the radius r, perpendicular height H and slant height h related?

questm6-height#42.en: The slant h is the longest side (opposite the right angle), so it sits alone as the c in a² + b² = c².

questm6-height#43.en: h² = H² + r² — the slant is the hypotenuse.

questm6-height#44.en: legs r and H, hypotenuse h → h² = H² + r²

questm6-height#45.en: To find a square pyramid's perpendicular height from the slant height of a face, what is the bottom of the right-angled triangle?

questm6-height#50.en: The slant runs to the MIDDLE of a base edge, so the bottom leg only reaches halfway across — ½ℓ.

questm6-height#51.en: Half the base side, ½ℓ — the slant meets the base at the midpoint of an edge.

questm6-height#52.en: h² = H² + (ℓ/2)²  →  bottom leg is ½ℓ, not the whole ℓ

questm6-height#53.en: In the right-angled triangle inside this solid, is the slant height the hypotenuse (the longest side)?

questm6-height#54.en: The right angle sits between the radius and the perpendicular height, so the side opposite it is the slant.

questm6-height#55.en: Yes — the slant is opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse and the longest of the three.

questm6-height#56.en: right angle between r and H → slant is the hypotenuse, so slant > H and slant > r
